# Initialisation
First access required modules.
```{julia}
using Compose, Colors, Measures
import Cairo, Fontconfig, Gadfly
import EpidemicsCFTP
epi = EpidemicsCFTP ; gf = Gadfly ;
```

For a laconic description of the `julia` package `Compose.jl` 
(the graphics package used for these figures),
see
<https://giovineitalia.github.io/Compose.jl/latest/>.
Further useful information is given in
<https://shashi.biz/ijulia-notebooks/funcgeo/>.

Basic simulation parameters are the `population` size 
and the `duration` (assume epidemic simulation commences at time `0`).
Note that (trivial) labelling issues arise if `population > MAXPOP=20`.
```{julia}
const population = 5 ;
const duration   = 2 ;
const MAXPOP  = 20 ;
if population > MAXPOP
  error("`population` exceeds `$(MAXPOP)`: modify code indexing time-lines!")
end ;
```

Set up and establish graphics size, coordinates, and drawing region.
```{julia}
set_default_graphic_size(6inch, 3.25inch) ;
coordinates = UnitBox(0, population, duration, -population, 
                      leftpad=0.5inch, rightpad=0.5inch, toppad=0.25inch) ;
REGION      = (context(), rectangle(), fill(colorant"bisque"), fillopacity(0.3)) ;
```


# Basic image template elements
We define a function to draw the time axis, with tick marks at integer times.
Note, both here and following, the careful use of graphics area units (`cx`, `cy`).
```{julia}
function time_axis(duration; tic=-0.2cy, xht=0.5cy)
  labellocs = [(x)cx for x in 0:duration]
  step = 10^floor(Int, log10(duration))
  tic_loc1  = [(((x)cx,xht), ((x)cx, xht+tic))    for x in 0:1.0step:duration]
  tic_loc2  = [(((x)cx,xht), ((x)cx, xht+tic))    for x in 0:0.5step:duration]
  tic_loc3  = [(((x)cx,xht), ((x)cx, xht+0.5tic)) for x in 0:0.1step:duration]

  (context(), # Returned value of function!
    (context(), text(labellocs, [xht + 0.25inch], ["$i" for i in 0:duration], 
      [hcenter], [vcenter]), fontsize(5pt), font("TimesRoman"), ),
    (context(), line([(0cx, xht), ((duration)cx, xht)]),
      stroke("grey"), linewidth(0.5mm) ),
    (context(), line(tic_loc1), stroke("grey"), linewidth(0.2mm)),
    (context(), line(tic_loc2), stroke("grey"), linewidth(0.1mm)),
    (context(), line(tic_loc3), stroke("grey"), linewidth(0.1mm)), )
end ;
```


Now we define a function to draw all time-lines as black threads labelled by circled integers.
```{julia}
function time_threads(duration, population)
  circlabels   = [string(Char(0x00002460+i-1)) for i in 1:population]

  (context(), # Returned value of function!
    (context(), text([0cx-0.25inch], [(k)cy for k in 1:population], circlabels,
      [hleft], [vcenter]), fontsize(10pt), font("TimesRoman"), ),
    (context(), line([[(0cx, (k)cy), ((duration)cx, (k)cy)] for k in 1:population]), 
      stroke("grey"), linewidth(0.5mm), ), )
end ;
```


::: {.callout-caution}
The definition of `circlabels` below needs to be changed if `population > MAXPOP=20`,
as unicode then runs out of circled integers!
(Figure out how to use 
one of the many ideas in <https://tex.stackexchange.com/questions/7032/good-way-to-make-textcircled-numbers#>.)
:::


A third function constructs scaffolding (axes, time lines _etc_).
```{julia}
function scaffolding(duration, population ; tic=-0.2cy, xht=0.5cy, region=REGION)
  (context(), region, time_axis(duration; tic=-tic, xht=xht), time_threads(duration, population))
end ;
```

# Dealing with different kinds of incident
Here is a function which creates a union of all composite types
below a given (typically abstract!) type. This is applied to create
a union type for composite types implementing `AbstractIncident`,
in order to be programmatic about construction of generalized 
drawing functions.
```{julia}
function unionize_composites(a::Type)::Type
  xl = Type[x for x in subtypes(a)]
  if length(xl) == 0
    return a # return a composite type
  else
    xl = Type[unionize_composites(y) for y in xl]
    return reduce((t1, t2) -> Union{t1, t2}, xl) # return a union type
  end
end

BasicIncident = unionize_composites(epi.AbstractIncident) ;
```

Various types of incident are styled by `julia` dictionaries and variables.
```{julia}
E = epi.AbstractIncident ; A = epi.AbstractInfection ; 
I = epi.Infection ; P = epi.PInfection ; R = epi.Removal ; C = epi.CRemoval
RADIUS   = 0.2cy ; SMRADIUS = 0.75RADIUS
BIT      = -0.02h
col = Dict(
  I => colorant"orange",  P => colorant"darkgreen",
  R => colorant"tan",     C => colorant"purple",
  A => colorant"yellow",  "blank" => colorant"white",
) ;
lw = Dict(
  "bdry"   =>  linewidth(1.00mm),   "trail"  =>  linewidth(0.75mm),
  "active" =>  linewidth(0.75mm),   "dormant" => linewidth(0.25mm),
) ;
```

Colour list: see <https://juliagraphics.github.io/Colors.jl/stable/namedcolors/>.

# An innovation for an unconditioned \(\SIR\) epidemic
Consider lists of potential incidents underlying
an unconditional epidemic.
```{julia}
env0 = epi.Innovation(5, 
  A[I(0.11,2,3), I(0.2,2,5), P(0.4,1,2), I(0.5,2,5), I(0.6,2,4), I(0.85,3,4), 
    I(0.9,2,3), I(1.0,2,5), P(1.1,2,3), I(1.05,4,5), I(1.2,2,4), I(1.6,3,5), 
    I(1.5,3,4)], 
  R[R(0.3,5), R(0.42,3), R(0.7,3), R(0.55,3), R(0.95,5), R(1.4,2), R(1.55,1),
    R(1.85,2)],
  C[C(1.3,2), C(0.8,1), C(1.7,4), C(1.8,4), C(1.92,5)] ) ;
```

Here are functions to draw inactive (respectively, active) nodes for each of a list
conposed of incidents from a prescribed composite type of `BasicIncident`. 
Variants
deal with `AbstractIncident[]` vectors by doing nothing -- useful if a
selected sublist is empty, so becoming an `AbstractIncident[]` vector.
```{julia}
function draw_incident(xl::Vector{T}; radius=RADIUS) where T<:BasicIncident
  (context(),
    (context(),
      text(map(x -> (x.t)cx, xl), map(x -> (x.target)cy, xl), 
           map(x -> string(x), xl), [hcenter], [vcenter]), 
      fontsize(5pt), font("Helvetica")),
    (context(),
      circle(map(x -> (x.t)cx, xl), map(x -> (x.target)cy, xl), [radius]), 
      fill(col["blank"]), stroke(col[eltype(xl)])), )
end

function draw_realized(xl::Vector{T}; radius=RADIUS, smradius=SMRADIUS) where T<:BasicIncident
  xtype = eltype(xl) ;
  (context(),
    (context(),
    circle(map(x -> (x.t)cx, xl), map(x -> (x.target)cy, xl), [radius]), 
    lw["active"], fill(col[xtype]), fillopacity(0.2), stroke(col[xtype]) ),
    if xtype<:epi.AbstractInfection
      (context(),
      circle(map(x->(x.t)cx, xl), map(x -> x.infectee, xl), [smradius]),
       lw["active"], fill(col[xtype]), fillopacity(0.5), stroke(col[xtype]))
    end, )
end ;

function draw_connect(xl::Vector{T}; bit=BIT, radius=RADIUS, active=false) where T<:BasicIncident
  xtype = eltype(xl)
  if ! (xtype<:epi.AbstractInfection)
    return
  end
  (context(), 
    line(map(x -> [((x.t)cx, (x.target)cy+radius), ((x.t)cx, (x.infectee)cy)], xl)),
    line(map(x -> [((x.t)cx - 0.3bit, (x.infectee)cy-bit), 
                   ((x.t)cx,          (x.infectee)cy), 
                   ((x.t)cx + 0.3bit, (x.infectee)cy-bit)], xl)), 
    stroke(col[xtype]), (active ? lw["active"] : lw["dormant"]) )
end

function draw_incident(xl::Vector{T}) where T<:epi.AbstractIncident end
function draw_realized(xl::Vector{T}) where T<:epi.AbstractIncident end
function draw_connect(xl::Vector{T}; active=false) where T<:epi.AbstractIncident end ;
```

We now add graphical depictions of the potential incidents supplied by the innovation.
Elements are plotted in reverse-order: for example, the first in sequence overlays 
all subsequent elements. @fig-potential illustrates the required plot.
```{julia}
elements = (context(),
  draw_incident([inc for inc in env0.infections if isa(inc, I)]),
  draw_incident([inc for inc in env0.infections if isa(inc, P)]),
  draw_incident([inc for inc in env0.removals   if isa(inc, R)]),
  draw_incident([inc for inc in env0.cremovals  if isa(inc, C)]),
  draw_connect([inc for inc in env0.infections  if isa(inc, I)]),
  draw_connect([inc for inc in env0.infections  if isa(inc, P)]), )
InitialView = compose(context(units=coordinates), 
  elements, 
  scaffolding(duration, population)) ;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-potential
#| fig-cap: "Potential incidents (both removals and infections):                        \
#|           Removals (R for _removal_) are blue outline disks;                         \
#|           conditional removals (C for _conditioned_) are purple outline disks;       \
#|           Infections (I for _infected_) are orange outline disks;                    \
#|           perpetuated infections (P for _perpetuated_) are dark green outline disks. \
#|           Orange arrows connect infector time-lines                                  \
#|           to corresponding infectee time-lines.                                      \
#|           Each disk is annotated by a summary description of its incident."
draw(PNG("image/InitialView.png"), InitialView)
draw(PDF("image/InitialView.pdf"), InitialView)
InitialView
```

# Evolving the epidemic in process time
Now plot epidemics using the time-sequence `chron` of potential incidents, 
derived
from the innovation using the `chronology` function. Compute trajectory
and history of realized incidents corresponding to a specific initial state at time \(0.0\),
given by an `SIR` structure. 
Then `evolution_recurse!`
works destructively on inputs, delivers the \(\SIR\) trajectory `traj`,
and realized incidents in `active`.

Use the `traj` argument to produce a plot against time of the numbers of
susceptibles, infectives and removed individuals, _via_ a dataframe
of trajectories as knots of piecewise constant functions.
```{julia}
using DataFrames
initial= epi.SIR(0.0, 4, 1, 0)
chron  = epi.chronology(env0) ; states = [initial] # both will be overwritten
traj, active = epi.evolution_recurse!(states, epi.AbstractIncident[], duration, chron)
t = [state.t for state in traj] ; push!(t, duration)
t = repeat(t, inner=2)[2:(end-1)]
s = repeat([state.s for state in traj], inner=2)
i = repeat([state.i for state in traj], inner=2)
r = repeat([state.r for state in traj], inner=2)
flow = DataFrame(t=t, Susceptibles=s, Infectives=i, Removals=r) ;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
print(flow) ;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Trajectories of susceptibles, infectives (brown dashed lines), \
#|           removals (grey dotted lines)."   
inf_layer = gf.layer(flow, x=:t, y=:Infectives, color=[col[I]], 
  gf.Geom.line, gf.style(line_width=1mm, line_style=[:solid]))
rem_layer = gf.layer(flow, x=:t, y=:Removals, color=[col[R]], 
  gf.Geom.line, gf.style(line_width=1mm, line_style=[:dash]))
sus_layer = gf.layer(flow, x=:t, y=:Susceptibles, color=[colorant"grey"], 
  gf.Geom.line, gf.style(line_width=1mm, line_style=[:dot]))
gf.plot(sus_layer, rem_layer, inf_layer,
  gf.style(panel_fill=colorant"bisque"), gf.Guide.xlabel("process time"), 
  gf.Guide.ylabel("removals, infectives, susceptibles", orientation=:vertical))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
In the following, it would be helpful to have a function calling `evolution_recurse!` which is non-destructive of its arguments!
:::


Now examine which of the potential incidents have been realized. 
Amend @fig-potential: realized incident nodes have light-coloured backgrounds and 
thicker line-widths, producing @fig-realized.

```{julia}
active_removals   = [inc for inc in active if (isa(inc, R) || isa(inc, C))]
observed_removals = [(k, inc) for (k, inc) in enumerate(active_removals) 
                       if k + initial.r < inc.target]

realized = (context(),
  draw_realized([inc for inc in active if isa(inc, I)]),
  draw_realized([inc for inc in active if isa(inc, P)]),
  draw_realized([inc for inc in active if isa(inc, C)]),
  draw_connect([inc for inc in active if isa(inc, I)]; active=true),
  draw_connect([inc for inc in active if isa(inc, P)]; active=true), )

removal_connections = (context(), # COuld this be cleaned up?
  (context(),          # Connecting removal nodes
    circle([(inc.t)cx for (k, inc) in observed_removals], 
           [(k + initial.r)cy for (k, inc) in observed_removals],
           [SMRADIUS]), stroke(col[C]), 
           lw["active"], fill(col[C]), fillopacity(0.5) ),
  (context(),          # Connecting removal lines
    line([[((inc.t)cx, (inc.target)cy - RADIUS), 
           ((inc.t)cx, (k + initial.r)cy + RADIUS)]
      for (k, inc) in observed_removals]), 
    stroke(col[R]), lw["trail"], strokedash([0.5mm, 0.5mm]) )
)

removed_fill = [(a,b) for (a,b) in zip(t, r) if b>0]
push!(removed_fill, (duration, 1))
infected_fill = [(a,b) for (a,b) in zip(t, i+r) if b>0]
removed1_fill = [(a,b + 1) for (a,b) in zip(t, r) if b < population]
append!(infected_fill, reverse(removed1_fill))

timelines = (context(),
  (context(),          # Trail of Removals
    line([(a,b) for (a,b) in zip(t, r) if b>0]),
    line([[(a,b), (duration, b)] for (a,b) in zip(t, r) if b>0]),
    stroke(col[R]), lw["bdry"] ),
  (context(),          # Removals trail fill
    polygon(removed_fill),
    fill(col[R]), fillopacity(0.1) ),
    
  (context(),          # Trail of Epidemic
    line([zip(t, i+r)]),
    line([[(a,b), (duration, b)] for (a,b) in zip(t, i+r) if b>0]),
    stroke(col[A]), lw["bdry"] ),
  (context(),          # Epidemic trail fill
    polygon(infected_fill),
    fill(col[A]), stroke(col[A]), fillopacity(0.1) ), )

FinalView = compose(context(units=coordinates), removal_connections, realized, 
           elements, timelines, scaffolding(duration, population)) ;
```

# Computing the last viable epidemic
First establish active removal incidents in time-decreasing order
of _removed_ timeline,
and list prior potential infections 
corresponding according to the time-line
they might infect (prior to removal of that time-line).
Notice we have not yet covered the possibility that some time-lines
are never infected and others are not removed before `duration`
(the end of the simulation). Notice too that the first time-line
is (of course) never infected.

```{julia}
active_removals = filter(x -> (isa(x, R) || isa(x, C)), active)
reversed_removals = reverse(collect(enumerate(active_removals)))
for (k, rem) in reversed_removals
  println("Timeline $k ends at $rem, at time $(rem.t)")
  prior_removals = [pr for pr in env0.removals if pr.target==k && pr.t < rem.t]
  println("  (prior rem) ", join([string(pr) for pr in prior_removals], " "))
  prior_infections = [pi for pi in env0.infections if pi.infectee==k && pi.t < rem.t]
  println("  (prior inf) ", join([string(pi) for pi in prior_infections], " "))
  println("\n")
end
```

By the nature of the simulation, no prior potential infections will infect
a time-line _after_ it has been removed, because by then the `target` time-line
must also have been removed.

::: {.callout-tip}

4. Tighten up so subsequent timelines also infected(!)
